rv.q: No matter how many innocent people they kill, this musical’s Bonnie and Clyde remain—like the show itself—not great, but not that bad.
Also, this is Wildhorn's most developed, most genuinely theatrical score.
For all that, three exciting performances and a better-than-usual score from Frank Wildhorn combine to make this an arresting if problematic new musical.
And so a musical about living on the edge ends up being safe.
But Clyde, honey, t’ain’t nothing you can do to raise the pulse of something that’s as near to dead as the show you’re in.
But the composer and lyricist show little flair for marrying story with song.

That so yawn-inducing a show has come to Broadway after runs at California's La Jolla Playhouse and Florida's Theatre, two of America's top regional theaters, proves only that when it comes to musicals, even the smartest producers can be struck dumb by wishful thinking.
A pop romance about the American nightmare, “Bonnie and Clyde” is solidly entertaining.
The show's young stars sing powerfully, and give spirited performances, even if they're not provided depths to plumb.
Bonnie and Clyde has many virtues but also enough flaws to keep it from blowing you away.
Wildhorn's Bonnie & Clyde aims for kiss-kiss-bang-bang, but too often it's just firing blanks.
The musical offers some stirring moments, but ultimately feels more like a series of vignettes than a cohesive theatrical experience.
Bonnie & Clyde is entangled in its own musical format, watering down the storytelling and, with it, the tension.

Yet in spite of a mostly pleasant country-and-blues score and strong, sexy performances from the doll-faced Laura Osnes and heartthrob Jeremy Jordan, this remains a problematic show that lacks focus and tends to pause and meander too often.
Whatever made Bonnie and Clyde special is missing from this sentimental musical, as are sufficient character development, adequate dramatic thrust, and any kind of subtext.
The show occasionally jolts but it generally fails to electrify viewers or inspire much pity for its hard-luck protagonists.

cn.t: Critics find this Depression-era outlaw musical safe and forgettable despite strong leads Laura Osnes and Jeremy Jordan. Wildhorn's score and the paint-by-numbers storytelling fail to capture the danger of the infamous duo.

sg.ra: Shubert/SeatPlan place rows C-E as 'just right' — close enough to catch facial detail without the stage-height skew that rows AA/A suffer inside this shallow 26'9" proscenium house; TickPick singles out row B (seats 105-110) as the best seat in the Schoenfeld.

SeatPlan notes the mezzanine overhang starts at row J but only begins clipping the top of the stage at row Q — so K-P sits in the narrow band that's still unobstructed yet priced below premium; TickPick and Headout independently flag K-P as the value pocket in this 1,079-seat Shubert house.

sg.vl: Overhang cuts the top of the stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly says rows beyond Q lose the top of the stage to the mezzanine overhang, and Headout/TickPick corroborate that under-overhang seats 'might have obstructed views from the overhang of the box seats or the mezzanine itself' — a real issue in this shallow Shubert house where the mezz projects forward.

sg.vl: Overhead sweep of the whole stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both cite front center mezz rows A-B as offering 'excellent overhead views perfect for appreciating the stage in one sweep' — the Schoenfeld's mezz hangs closer to the stage than larger Shubert houses, so row A feels surprisingly close rather than distant.

SeatPlan flags E-G as benefiting from 'great rake for aerial views which cover the entire stage below' — the Schoenfeld mezz is steeper than most Shubert houses, so E-G keeps the full stage visible where a flatter rake would start clipping; Headout calls it a value tier below the premium A-D band.

Multiple sources describe rear mezz past row F as 'a gamble... actors start to look like LEGO figures' — despite the Schoenfeld only having 392 mezz seats, the steep rake trades sightline for proximity and you lose emotional read on faces; a J104 reviewer conceded 'nearly center, no obstructions' but 2nd-to-last row.

SeatPlan notes 'single-digit seats in rows A-D' of the side mezz 'are more directly above the stage and feel surprisingly close' — the Schoenfeld's narrow 40-foot proscenium means side-mezz angles are less punishing than wider houses, though TickPick warns the far edges of rows 'have slightly blocked views of the corners of the stage'.
